newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian election campaign kicks off peacefully.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian election campaign kicks off peacefully.

text.p: Indonesian political leaders spread out through the sprawling archipelago on Sunday at the start of a month-long general election campaign to woo nearly 125 million voters in the world's fourth-largest nation.
Leaders including President Suharto and armed forces chief General Feisal Tanjung have called for a peaceful campaign and there were no reports of trouble in the initial stages.
The only three parties legally permitted to contest the May 29 local and national elections have agreed to campaign each day in separate areas of the country.

On Sunday, the ruling Golkar was campaigning across the country's most populous island of Java and in the remote Mulukus and Irian Jaya in the east. Golkar is seeking over 70 percent of the vote after taking 68 percent in the last elections in 1992.
The Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), which won 17 percent of the vote in 1992, was campaigning in Sumatra, the resort island of Bali and its adjacent Nusa Tenggara islands.

The Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party, badly split since its leader Megawati Sukarnoputri was ousted by government-backed rebels last year, was seeking voter backing in Kalimantan on Borneo island and Sulawesi. It took 15 percent in 1992.

President Suharto's eldest daughter, businesswoman Siti Hardyanti Rukmana (also known as Tutut), kicked off the Golkar campaign in populous central Java with a mass rally at a fairground in the industrial port city of Semarang with a population of 750,000.
Reuter correspondent Jim Della-Giacoma reported that about 10,000 people were at the fairground when Tutut arrived wearing a blouse and skirt in Golkar's yellow colours.
A huge banner was draped around a Ferris wheel on one side of the fairground proclaiming "Golkar is my choice".
Central Java was awash with yellow banners, vastly outnumbering the green symbol of the United Development Party and the red of the PDI.
Security was low-key with few troops in evidence. Golkar officials were providing the main security at the Semarang rally.
Indonesian markets were jittery last week on fears of possible campaign violence. The rupiah dropped 20 points to 2,440.50 to the dollar before moving back to 2,436 by Saturday.
The Jakarta Stock Exchange was little changed on Friday, with the composite index closing at 652.4 points, but brokers attributed some profit-taking to election nerves.

"The crucial point is Sunday and Monday. People are looking at the start of the campaign which should give indications whether the authorities have things under control," a foreign exchange dealer said.
